claims.text: High-entropy nanoparticles maintain a stable single-phase structure across 473–1923 K.
High configurational mixing entropy thermodynamically stabilizes the homogeneous solid solution at elevated temperatures.
Favorable intermetallic interactions thermodynamically stabilize the homogeneous solid solution.
Kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion retard phase segregation as temperature increases.
The tested nanoparticles contain at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially form a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
The nanoparticles will be subjected to in situ high-temperature treatment from 473 K to 1923 K under simultaneous catalytic and thermoelectric stimuli.
Environmental TEM and synchrotron XRD will be used to monitor the treatment.
The balance between intermetallic interaction energies and barriers to atomic diffusion mediates homogeneous-phase retention.
If kinetic barriers counter temperature-induced diffusion sufficiently, the nanoparticles remain structurally and chemically stable.
The nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous phase and uniform elemental distribution during testing.
Phase segregation will be minimal or delayed relative to lower-entropy or less kinetically stabilized systems.
The initial homogeneous single-phase state will be confirmed by ex situ characterization before high-temperature testing.
The prediction is expected to hold under controlled catalytic and thermoelectric environments and controlled temperature ramps within 473–1923 K.
Large changes in gas composition or rapid temperature ramps may break down kinetic stabilization and alter phase stability.
The relative contributions of thermodynamic stabilization and kinetic delay may vary with nanoparticle size, composition, and operating parameters.
Binary or ternary nanoparticles will serve as a lower-entropy control under otherwise identical conditions.
Significant phase segregation or elemental redistribution under the defined conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
